title: The future of games could kill the future of games
gist: AI datacentre demand has pushed DDR5 memory prices up 400-500 per cent since September 2025, forcing console makers to strip cost: Microsoft cut 3,200 Xbox staff (a fifth of the division) and Sony will end physical disc production for new PlayStation games from January 2028, implying a discless PS6. The author argues the resulting price rises and loss of ownership rights could make the incumbent PlayStation 5 the most attractive console of 2028.

themes.theme: AI-driven memory cost shock hits hardware

insights.claim: The price of DDR5 RAM used in games consoles has risen roughly 400 to 500 per cent since September 2025, up from about 300 per cent as of March 2026, because AI infrastructure buildout competes for the same memory supply.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Hard consumer-side evidence of the AI memory squeeze: long memory makers, but expect margin compression or price rises across all RAM-dependent consumer hardware.
insights.locator: First, there is the necessity of it all

insights.claim: Console makers including Sony are cutting hardware content wherever possible in response to component price shocks, with the disc drive an obvious target because removing it saves both drive hardware and the manufacturing and distribution of discs.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Component inflation transmits into product de-featuring before it shows up as headline price rises — watch BOM stripping as an early inflation indicator.
insights.locator: Thanks to these price shocks, console makers

insights.claim: The forthcoming PlayStation 6 is likely to be more expensive than any prior PlayStation, with rising console prices attributed to the same AI-driven component costs.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Higher console entry prices compress the installed-base growth that games publishers' revenue models assume — a demand risk for software as well as hardware.
insights.locator: But at a time of rising console prices

insights.claim: The most attractive console of 2028 may end up being the existing PlayStation 5 rather than any new hardware, as players stick with libraries they already own instead of paying up for the next generation.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A stalled console upgrade cycle would extend the current-gen tail and hit next-gen hardware and launch-title forecasts — check console attach and refresh assumptions.
insights.quote: The hottest console of 2028 may end up being the current PlayStation 5.
insights.locator: How many players are going to ignore the next shiny thing

themes.theme: Xbox retrenchment after the acquisition binge

insights.claim: Microsoft's Xbox division, under new leadership, announced layoffs of 3,200 workers in early July 2026, about a fifth of its staff, a scale shocking even to an industry used to job cuts.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A fifth of a division cut signals Microsoft is treating gaming as a cost-optimisation problem, not a growth engine — reprice its consumer segment accordingly.
insights.locator: A couple of weeks ago, under its new leadership

insights.claim: Microsoft's Xbox cuts extend to divesting entire game studios acquired during the boom, which must now continue their existing projects without Microsoft's long-term support.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Forced studio divestments create distressed acquisition opportunities and raise execution risk on in-flight AAA pipelines.
insights.locator: Xbox’s axe extends to entire games studios

insights.claim: The multi-billion-dollar acquisitions made by the largest games companies have not yet paid off, and pandemic-era hiring sprees have inverted into today's firing sprees as at-home spending on games normalised.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Classic demand-pull-forward unwind: treat pandemic-cohort headcount and M&A in any consumer-digital sector as a structural overhang, not a one-off.
insights.quote: the hiring sprees of the pandemic (when everyone was indoors and spending time and money on games) became the firing sprees of today (when they are not)
insights.locator: It’s a number that’s shocking even to an industry

themes.theme: Sony's discless pivot and the digital-only endgame

insights.claim: Sony announced in early July 2026 that it will stop producing physical discs for new PlayStation games from January 2028, which also implies the coming PlayStation 6 will have no disc drive.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A dated end-of-life for boxed console software: negative for physical games retail and disc replication, positive for platform-store take rates.

insights.claim: Almost 80 per cent of the games Sony sold last year were digital rather than disc-based, a complete reversal of the ratio ten years earlier, according to Sony's own financial reporting.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: The 80/20 digital mix explains why platform owners can afford to abandon physical — and why storefront economics now dominate console profitability.

insights.claim: Digital distribution collapses per-unit cost to effectively one server copy that users download, eliminating manufacturing and logistics from the cost of goods for games.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: The margin arithmetic that makes the digital shift irreversible regardless of consumer preference — assume platforms keep pushing it.
insights.quote: A digital game is, in effect, a single copy on a server that people download to their home consoles.
insights.locator: Not only would disclessness save on the drive hardware

insights.claim: Rockstar Games disclosed a week before Sony's announcement that boxed physical editions of Grand Theft Auto VI will contain download codes rather than actual discs.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: The biggest publisher moving first de-risks Sony's disc exit and confirms publishers, not just platforms, are driving disintermediation of retail.
insights.locator: A week before Sony made its own announcement

insights.claim: Grand Theft Auto VI is due for release later in 2026 and is expected to be enormous in both financial and cultural terms, even against the industry's weakening backdrop.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: A single 2026 title could mask sector-wide deterioration in aggregate revenue data — strip it out when assessing underlying games demand.
insights.locator: the release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) later this year

insights.claim: Buyers of digital games acquire a revocable licence rather than ownership, so a platform can remove a title from a user's library for censorship reasons, commercial disputes with developers, or simply because supporting older releases is no longer worthwhile.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Licence-not-ownership is a latent regulatory and reputational liability for platforms as physical alternatives disappear — a plausible future consumer-protection intervention.
insights.quote: With most digital media, you’re not actually buying ownership rights to the thing itself, but a licence to use it—and that licence can be rescinded.
insights.locator: Perhaps the greatest benefit of discs

insights.claim: Physical discs deliver economic functions downloads cannot — resale, lending, sharing, charity-shop and library circulation — meaning the digital shift quietly destroys the secondary market for games.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Killing resale raises effective per-title cost to consumers and removes a competing supply channel — structurally positive for publisher pricing power.
insights.locator: After all, discs do many things that downloads do not

insights.claim: Sony's discless announcement triggered a sustained social-media backlash, with thousands of complaint comments under every July product post and one 'Fuck Sony' protest comment spelt out in disc cases reaching 1.2m views.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Quantified brand-damage signal ahead of a premium hardware launch — watch whether goodwill erosion shows up in PS6 preorder conversion.
insights.locator: Ever since Sony confirmed its discless future

insights.claim: Industry analyst Daniel Ahmad notes that even as the digital ratio passes 80 per cent the residual 20 per cent still represents tens of millions of buyers, with almost 70m PlayStation discs sold last year.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Sizes the abandoned segment at roughly 70m units a year — a real revenue pool being ceded, and a hook for a rival positioning on physical media.
insights.quote: the digital ratio is set to surpass 80%, but that 20% is still 10s of millions
insights.locator: As the industry analyst Daniel Ahmad puts it

insights.claim: Rational unit economics and consumer sentiment are diverging in games, so decisions that are financially unavoidable are still generating measurable ill will that may depress future spending.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Cost-driven product decisions can be individually correct and collectively value-destroying — a watch-item for platform churn and engagement metrics.
insights.quote: Facts, however, are not the same as feelings.
insights.locator: Facts, however, are not the same as feelings

themes.theme: Scale versus fragility in the games industry

insights.claim: Video games generate more revenue than movies and music combined, no single entertainment product has grossed more than Grand Theft Auto V, and Minecraft's monthly player count exceeds the population of all but seven countries.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Sets the scale baseline: games is the largest entertainment category, so its cost shocks and layoffs are a macro-relevant consumer-tech signal, not a niche one.
insights.locator: It used to be the case that, when talking to people

insights.claim: The persuasion problem about games has inverted: the industry's scale is now obvious while its weakness and vulnerability are what need explaining, with the author having argued since March 2026 that the most successful form of entertainment is failing.
insights.speaker: Peter Hoskin
insights.so_what: Sector-level bearish framing from a specialist critic: revenue size is masking deteriorating unit economics across platform holders and studios.
insights.quote: The most successful form of entertainment is failing
insights.locator: Nowadays, though, the problem is the other way around
